title: Local variables
recap: Local variables have block scope: their names are usable from the point of declaration through the end of the block that contains them. A nested block can access a variable from an enclosing block, but the enclosing block cannot access a local declared only in the nested block.

Ordinary local variables have automatic storage duration, so they are created at their definitions and destroyed when execution leaves their blocks. Defining a variable in the smallest existing scope that needs it reduces the amount of state a reader must track.
objectives: Declare an outer local that remains usable after a nested block.
Declare a temporary local in the smallest block that needs it.
Use both outer and inner locals while both are in scope.
Report the surviving outer value after the inner local's lifetime ends.
warnings: A local variable cannot be used before its declaration or after its block ends.
Names in the same scope must be unique.
Do not create an otherwise unnecessary block solely to shorten a variable's lifetime in production code; a function may be clearer.
challenge: Create itemsRemaining as a local initialized to 9. In the supplied nested block, define packedItems as a const local initialized to 4, subtract it from itemsRemaining, and print it. After packedItems has gone out of scope, print the updated itemsRemaining.
hints: itemsRemaining must be declared in main's outer block because it is used after the nested block.
Declare const int packedItems{ 4 }; inside the nested block immediately before using it.
Update the outer variable with itemsRemaining -= packedItems while both names are in scope.
